TECHNICAL POINT OF CONTACT (TPOC)

  • Army xTech MailboxClick to show information

PROJECTED CMMC LEVEL REQUIREMENT

Level 1

TECHNOLOGY AREAS

Air Platform  |  Battlespace  |  Bio Medical  |  Chem Bio Defense  |  Electronics  |  Human Systems  |  Information Systems  |  Materials  |  Sensors  |  Space Platforms  |  Weapons

MODERNIZATION PRIORITIES

Advanced Computing and Software  |  Advanced Materials  |  Biotechnology  |  Human-Machine Interfaces  |  Hypersonics  |  Integrated Network Systems-of-Systems  |  Integrated Sensing and Cyber  |  Microelectronics  |  Quantum Science  |  Trusted AI and Autonomy

KEYWORDS

xTech; Autonomy; Robotics; Uncrewed Ground Vehicles (UGV); Uncrewed Aerial Systems (UAS); Teleoperation; Contested Environments; GPS-Denied Navigation; Communications-Denied, Degraded, Intermittent, and Limited (DDIL) Environments; Electronic Warfare (EW) Resiliency Force Sustainment, Contested Logistics; Point-of-Need Delivery

OBJECTIVE

The U.S. Army is seeking innovative force sustainment solutions from eligible small businesses across the U.S. through the xTech Kinetic Reach competition. This platform offers participants the opportunity to engage with the Department of War (DoW), earn prize money and submit a Direct to Phase II Army Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) proposal.

The U.S. Army FUZE xTech Program, in partnership with the U.S. Army Europe and Africa (USAREUR-AF) and Global Tactical Edge Acquisition Directorate (G-TEAD) is executing the xTech|Kinetic Reach competition as part of the G-TEAD Accelerated Capability Event (ACE) series. xTech|Kinetic Reach addresses the growing uncrewed aerial system (UAS) threat by identifying high-potential solutions and accelerating transition through funding and integration into live USAREUR-AF-led exercises. Integrating into a USAREUR-AF-led exercise is critical to: (1) validate capabilities under operationally realistic conditions, (2) inform acquisition and integration decisions, and (3) address near-term gaps in autonomous ground operations and effects delivery in contested environments.

The Army recognizes that the DoW must enhance engagements with U.S. small businesses by (1) understanding the spectrum of world-class technologies being developed commercially that may benefit the DoW; (2) integrating the sector of non-traditional innovators into the DoW Science and Technology (S&T) ecosystem; and (3) providing expertise and feedback to accelerate, mature, and transition technologies of interest to the DoW.

DESCRIPTION

xTech|Kinetic Reach is a focused open-topic competition designed to identify cutting-edge technology solutions that will drive significant advancements in military capabilities while addressing complex challenges and enhancing national security. In largescale combat operations, U.S. Army forces must sustain dispersed, continuously moving formations while operating inside highly contested environments characterized by persistent observation, long range fires, electromagnetic interference, degraded mobility corridors, and severely constrained logistics. Current sustainment and recovery methods rely heavily on manned systems that are increasingly vulnerable, slow to adapt, and unable to meet the demands of operations conducted near or within the Autonomous Zone. The Army requires a suite of interoperable, autonomous or minimally manned capabilities - spanning ground and air distribution, power generation, forward arming and refueling, and vehicle recovery - that can operate with minimal oversight, low signatures, reduced logistical burden, and seamless command and control (C2) integration. These capabilities must sustain tempo, reduce soldier exposure, and ensure survivability and mission continuity across the entire sustainment and recovery enterprise in high-threat, GPS and communications degraded environments where traditional methods are no longer feasible or survivable.

The Army is seeking to evaluate capabilities that demonstrate performance in one of six (6) capability areas, and meet the following criteria for its capability area:

Topic 1: Uncrewed Ground Payload Transportation

Topic 2: Autonomous container Handling/Movement System

Topic 3: Future Power Generation

Topic 4: Autonomous UAV/UGV Forward Arming and Refueling Point (FARP) System

Topic 5: Uncrewed Aerial Payload Transportation

Topic 6: Uncrewed, Automated, Ground Recovery System

Full competition details including details on these 6 topic areas of interest can be found in Appendix A section of the xTech|Kinetic Reach competition RFI here: https://www.xtech.army.mil/competitions/.

These capabilities must sustain tempo, reduce soldier exposure, and ensure survivability and mission continuity across the entire sustainment and recovery enterprise in high-threat, GPS and communications degraded environments where traditional methods are no longer feasible or survivable.

The Army is seeking to evaluate capabilities that demonstrate performance in one of six (6) capability areas, and meet the following criteria for its capability area:

Topic 1: Uncrewed Ground Payload Transportation

Topic 2: Autonomous container Handling/Movement System

Topic 3: Future Power Generation

Full competition details including details on these 6 topic areas of interest can be found in Appendix A section of the xTech|Kinetic Reach competition RFI here: https://www.xtech.army.mil/competitions/.

The U.S. Army intends to award up to $1,500,000 in cash prizes throughout the competition. Up to 15 finalists will be selected at the conclusion of the Part 1 evaluation period and will be provided the opportunity to participate in the Part 2 live Soldier exercise, anticipated to occur in November 2026. Finalists who attend the Soldier exercise will receive a cash prize of $25,000, following the event. Finalists who also participate and have their technology integrated in the exercise will receive an additional $25,000, following the event. Following completion of the exercise, up to five (5) final winners will be selected to receive an additional cash prize of $150,000 each. Final winners may be considered for potential follow-on agreements and contracting opportunities. Part 2 winners that qualify as U.S. Small Businesses will have the opportunity to submit a Direct to Phase II Army SBIR proposal worth up to $2,000,000.

PHASE I

This topic is accepting Direct-to-Phase II submissions with a cost limit of $2,000,000 and a period of performance of 12-18 months. Only winners of the xTech|Kinetic Reach competition are permitted to submit a proposal for this topic.  In order for proposers to submit a DP2 proposal, they must provide the justification documentation to substantiate that the scientific and technical merit and feasibility described above has been met and describes the potential military and/or commercial applications. Documentation should include all relevant information including, but not limited to: technical reports, test data, prototype designs/models, and performance goals/results.

PHASE II

Produce prototype solutions that will be easy to operate by a Soldier. These products will be provided to select Army units for testing and experimentation with end Users in a realistic field environment. Feedback from testing and experimentation will be provided directly to Small Businesses to iterate rapidly on recommended modifications or improvements for Army operational use. In addition, companies will work with Army partners to develop a draft technology transition and commercialization plan for DoW and commercial markets.

PHASE III DUAL USE APPLICATIONS

Complete the maturation of the company’s technology developed in Phase II to TRL 8/9 and produce prototypes to support scaling and fielding of the technology with the Army and pursue commercialization pathways.

REFERENCES

  1. https://www.xtech.army.mil/competitions/

Question Submitted On: 06/30/2026

Question:

At white-paper stage, are the heavy-payload movement thresholds (e.g., 22,000+ lb, 250+ km) evaluated at the integrated-system level, such that maturity evidence may reference the host platform's demonstrated performance?

Answer:

220VAC for commercial European power if a system needs to connect to an external grid. 

Question Submitted On: 06/30/2026

Question:

For Capability 1, is an offeror whose core contribution is the autonomy/software layer integrated onto a COTS or partner heavy-payload platform eligible to compete as a single applicant, or does this need to be structured and marked as an "integrated solution" on the registration page?

Answer:

If a company has something that can add autonomy, task intelligence, and GOAT-net integration onto an existing POR vehicle, we’d like to evaluate that and can work the coordination to have the right GFE present at the evaluation event in November. However, I think it’s a fair assessment that the evaluation criteria will prefer integrated solutions to bolt-on ones. 

  

Subject to the limits of our follow-on OTA, if a Vendor’s autonomy solution is better than another Vendor’s, but Vendor B has a better payload-movement capability, we’d want to make conditional offers subject to Vendor A and Vendor B partnering to pair their offerings prior to additional testing.

OBJECTIVE

The U.S. Army is seeking information from eligible small businesses across the U.S. to identify and advance commercialization pathways for a curated portfolio of high-potential Army Intellectual Property (IP) sets through the xTech|Inversion competition. This platform offers participants the opportunity to engage with the Department of War (DoW), earn prize money and submit a Phase I Army Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) proposal.

The Assistant Secretary of the Army for Acquisition, Logistics and Technology (ASA(ALT)) is partnering with the Office of the Deputy Under Secretary of the Army (DUSA) and the Deputy Assistant Secretary of the Army for Research and Technology (DASA R&T) to deliver the xTech|Inversion competition. The Army recognizes that the DoW must enhance engagements with U.S. small businesses by (1) understanding the spectrum of world-class technologies being developed commercially that may benefit the DoW; (2) integrating the sector of non-traditional innovators into the DoW Science and Technology (S&T) ecosystem; and (3) providing expertise and feedback to accelerate, mature, and transition technologies of interest to the DoW.

DESCRIPTION

xTech|Inversion is an open-topic competition designed to identify cutting-edge technology solutions that will drive significant advancements in military capabilities while addressing complex challenges and enhancing national security. The Army faces challenges in rapidly transitioning government-funded scientific breakthroughs into scalable, real-world solutions that address both military and commercial needs. Traditional pathways often limit access to innovative intellectual property and slow the pace of technology adoption. There is a critical need to foster stronger partnerships with non-traditional defense contractors, enabling them to leverage Army-developed intellectual property for dual-use applications. By bridging the gap between foundational research and market-driven innovation, the Army seeks to accelerate the development and deployment of technologies that address complex tactical challenges while also achieving commercial viability. Technologies that are selected from this competition to have the highest potential impact on the Army will have a structured pathway to continue developing those solutions for Army systems alongside Army customers. xTech|Inversion encourages submissions that may not be familiar with the Army problem your technology can solve, but can clearly articulate the solution's advantage, the technical viability, and commercial potential.

Full competition details including information on the available Army IP identified for this competition can be found in the Appendix A section of the xTech|Inversion competition RFI here: https://www.xtech.army.mil/competitions/.

The competition will award up to $1,000,000 in cash prizes throughout the competition to selected participants. Up to 12 finalists will receive a cash prize of $20,000 each and an opportunity to pitch their innovative technology solutions to a panel of Army and DoW subject matter experts (SMEs) in August 2026. The Army intends to select up to five (5) final winners of the competition to receive an additional cash prize of $150,000 each. Final winners may submit a Phase I Army SBIR proposal worth up to $300,000.

PHASE I

This topic is accepting Phase I submissions for a cost limit of $300,000 and a maximum 6-month period of performance. Only winners of the xTech|Inversion competition are permitted to submit a Phase I proposal for this topic.

Companies will complete a feasibility study that demonstrates the firm’s competitive technical advantage relative to other commercial products (if other products exist) and develop concept plans for how the company’s technology solution leveraging potential Army IP identified for this competition can be applied to Army modernization priority areas. Studies should clearly detail and identify a firm’s technology at both the individual component and system levels, provide supporting literature for technical feasibility, highlight existing performance data, showcase the technology’s application opportunities to a broad base of customers outside the defense space, a market strategy for the commercial space, how the technology directly addresses the Army’s modernization area as well as include a technology development roadmap to demonstrate scientific and engineering viability. At the end of Phase I, the company will be required to provide a concept demonstration of their technology to demonstrate a high probability that continued design and development will result in a fully realized prototype during Phase II.

PHASE II

Produce prototype solutions that will be easy to operate by a Soldier. These products will be provided to select Army units for testing and experimentation with end Users in a realistic field environment. Feedback from testing and experimentation will be provided directly to Small Businesses to iterate rapidly on recommended modifications or improvements for Army operational use. In addition, companies will work with Army partners to develop a draft technology transition and commercialization plan for DoW and commercial markets.

PHASE III DUAL USE APPLICATIONS

Complete the maturation of the company’s technology developed in Phase II to TRL 6-7 and produce prototypes to support scaling and fielding of the technology with the Army and pursue commercialization pathways leveraging potential IP license agreements from the Army.

REFERENCES

  1. https://www.xtech.army.mil/competitions/ 

Question Submitted On: 06/23/2026

Question:

Can Reactor 2 operate independently using an externally supplied ethylene stream, or is the integrated two-reactor configuration required for practical operation? 

Answer:

Yes, Reactor 2 can operate independently using an externally supplied ethylene stream.

Question Submitted On: 06/23/2026

Question:

Although methanol is listed among the potential oxygenated feedstocks in the patent, all experimental examples appear to be based on aqueous ethanol. Has the reactor architecture been experimentally evaluated using methanol feedstocks, or is methanol compatibility currently only conceptual? 

Answer:

No, we did not try the methanol. We were focusing on ethanol study.

Question Submitted On: 06/15/2026

Question:

What Technology Readiness Level (TRL) range is the Army targeting for participating solutions? 

Answer:

This competition is TRL agnostic. 

Question Submitted On: 06/15/2026

Question:

Is using a selected IP set as a module within a broader, company-owned product an acceptable approach, or does the proposal need to treat the IP set as a standalone product? 

Answer:

A company could choose to develop an ARL invention/patent as either a ‘module’ to add to or complement their own products/IP or a stand-alone product. Either way, companies will need to lay out/describe how they intend to use/commercialize the licensed government IP if and when they submit a formal patent license application. 

Question Submitted On: 06/15/2026

Question:

For IP set 8, how should applicants address the operational sustainment model, including lifecycle cost, readiness impact, maintenance forecasting, deployment economics, and audit-ready accountability?  

Answer:

Applicants should describe how the proposed solution supports long-term operation in field environments, including calibration stability, sensor reliability, installation and replacement requirements, and expected maintenance intervals. White papers should also address deployment and lifecycle costs, impact on operational readiness through reduced installation complexity or downtime, and approaches for data integrity, traceability, and auditability of power monitoring records. Quantitative estimates are encouraged where available. 

Question Submitted On: 06/15/2026

Question:

For the Phase I Army SBIR, does the proof of concept need to focus only on the IP set itself, or can it include integrating the IP set into the applicant's host platform as the demonstration?

Answer:

Either approach is feasible. The company should do what makes the most sense for them.

Question Submitted On: 06/15/2026

Question:

What intellectual property rights will participating companies retain, and what rights does the Army expect? 

Answer:

This depends on the company's intent and is best addressed through the patent license application process. Interested parties should reach out to the appropriate tech transfer office to discuss this further.

Question Submitted On: 06/15/2026

Question:

Can a small business acquire the patent license outside of the xTech Inversion program?

Answer:

Yes, you can apply for a license outside of this program. You should get in touch with the tech transfer office of the responsible Army laboratory.

Question Submitted On: 06/15/2026

Question:

How should applicants handle IP rights when combining Army-owned IP with their own developed software, data models, or algorithms?

Answer:

A licensing process would need to be followed. This will be covered in more detail during the finalist accelerator, but it involves submitting a patent license application.

Question Submitted On: 06/15/2026

Question:

For IP set 12, what about proposing an open architecture that can adapt to applications and specs that will be defined in the future?  

Answer:

Open architecture approaches are fine and often desirable, but only if they remain grounded in real converter physics and commercialization pathways. They should still define controllable boundaries—like topology choice, regulation method, and expected performance ranges—so we can assess feasibility and transition potential, not just conceptual flexibility. 

Question Submitted On: 06/15/2026

Question:

IP set 12, what is the physical form factor of the converter circuit?

Answer:

It was demonstrated on a rigid PCB, but other substrates are possible. The active part of the converter is very small, about 0.34 square inches (roughly the size of a dime).

Question Submitted On: 06/15/2026

Question:

IP set 12, what is the minimum input voltage the converter has been validated to step up from, and what is the output voltage range?

Answer:

The converter can self-start at less than 20 millivolts and provide an output of up to 2.5 volts. It has demonstrated a step-up from 35 millivolts input to a 2.5-volt output with over 400 microwatts of power at 58% efficiency. The desired output is typically regulated at 1.8 to 3.3 volts.

Question Submitted On: 06/15/2026

Question:

IP set 12, has this converter been tested in combination with IP Set 11 (Dual Coil Inductive Energy Generator)?

Answer:

No, they were developed separately and have not been tested together.

Question Submitted On: 06/15/2026

Question:

For IP set 12, how should the white paper address that the topics are very light on technical specs?  

Answer:

The white papers should explicitly treat missing technical specs as part of the problem definition. Participants are expected to make reasonable engineering assumptions for low-voltage step-up converters and clearly state them—especially input range, power levels, efficiency targets, and intended application domains. The quality signal is how well they define and justify a viable commercialization envelope, not whether they guess an exact spec correctly. 

Question Submitted On: 06/15/2026

Question:

Has the harvester been tested in any continuous low-G oscillation environment — vibration table, pendulum, or wrist-worn prototype — as opposed to single-event setback testing?

Answer:

Setback generators designed for fusing, need to keep an explosive round and it’s connected circuitry de-energized until it sees gun-launch.  The shear disc tightly confines the magnetic and it is help in the upper position until the gun-launch event shears the disk, allowing the magnet to displace.   

Small reserve batteries can deliver around 100 mW of power and the M203 flight duration is around 30 sec.  When setback generators approach this amount of energy interesting new applications are realized.  The maximum magnet velocity is around 10 m/s, thus a setback generator for an M203 maximum energy produced approaches 350 mJ of kinetic energy.   

Question Submitted On: 06/15/2026

Question:

What materials comprise the cylindrical enclosure, magnet, and coils — specifically whether any ferromagnetic materials are present that would interact with a brass or aluminum housing? 

Answer:

Cartech SS430F, Neodymium D42B-N52, coil was plastic, no brass or aluminum.  

Question Submitted On: 06/15/2026

Question:

IP set 12, the topic is light on technical specs. How should the white paper address this? Should we define the specs ourselves?

Answer:

The patent was written broadly. The technology was originally developed for wearable thermoelectric generators on skin. White papers should treat missing specs as part of the problem, state justified engineering assumptions, and define clear performance and physical boundaries so feasibility can be assessed. Open architecture approaches are acceptable.

Question Submitted On: 06/15/2026

Question:

For IP set 11, what is the output voltage and current profile of the generator?

Answer:

For the specified requirements, it charged a 120-microfarad capacitor to 13.7 volts. The power curve mimicked the gun-launch acceleration profile, and the coil winding resistance was approximately 0.7 ohms.

Question Submitted On: 06/15/2026

Question:

For IP set 11, what was the measured power output in laboratory testing?

Answer:

For the M203 platform, the generator produced 9 millijoules of energy, charging a 120-microfarad capacitor to 13.7 volts. For the higher velocity Mark 19 platform, it is estimated that 30 to 60 millijoules could be generated.

Question Submitted On: 06/15/2026

Question:

For IP set 11, what were the original design G-force parameters, and has any variant been tested at a lower acceleration threshold (e.g., 8-50G range)?

Answer:

The M203 and the Mk19 setback acceleration profiles were tested.  Two different shear disc designs were used for the respective gun-launch accelerations. Nothing lower than 11,000 g’s with a 1.25 ms pulse duration has been tested.  The magnet, in the non-displaced position, is tightly held in the upper magnetic loop where the magnetic flux is confined.  So 50 g’s might not be enough static acceleration to break the pull force of around 4 lbs.  This equates to roughly 1200 g’s. 

Question Submitted On: 06/15/2026

Question:

For IP set 4, Would the Army view predictive maintenance, cost/readiness analysis, and sustainment reporting as valuable commercialization extensions of the sensor technology?

Answer:

As a research lab, the Chemical Biological Center (CBC) would not perform these analyses at the R&D level. This would typically occur later when a technology transitions to a Program of Record. However, a patent licensing partner may choose to conduct this type of analysis as part of their business development.

Question Submitted On: 06/15/2026

Question:

Can the Army provide samples of the zirconium material or fibers during the Phase I feasibility effort?

If a sufficient sample amount exists, providing it under a commercial evaluation license could be discussed and possibly included in the license terms. Another option is a CRADA, which might require cost reimbursement, to fabricate the material.

Question Submitted On: 06/15/2026

Question:

Will awardees have access to the underlying fabrication methods and technical data associated with the zirconium hydroxide technology?

Answer:

A commercial evaluation license would cover data directly related to the patent. Discussing separate, underlying fabrication methods and data could be possible under a Cooperative Research and Development Agreement (CRADA), provided there is sufficient benefit to the Army. 

Question Submitted On: 06/15/2026

Question:

Can the zirconium hydroxide material be used as a coating on a chemical sensor for detection, rather than being incorporated into textiles?

Answer:

Using it as a sensor coating can certainly be considered and discussed. It has not been a topic the Army has pursued in depth, but a commercial evaluation license would allow for a more detailed discussion.

Question Submitted On: 06/15/2026

For software-focused small businesses, is the Army open to proposals that commercialize one of the Army IP sets by building a complementary software, analytics, governance, sustainment, or commercialization layer around the IP, rather than manufacturing the physical device or material itself?

We’re looking forward to seeing a range of creative and impactful solutions and discovering how your expertise can contribute to advancing Army initiatives.

Question Submitted On: 06/15/2026

Question:

Does the xTech Inversion competition allow for combining IP sets in one proposal?

Answer:

No, only one IP set should be submitted for each proposal, as outlined in the RFI.

Question Submitted On: 06/15/2026

Question:

What is the preferred way to disclose the pending proposal to the Program Office, as Section II directs?

Answer:

Email the disclosure to the xTech mailbox.

Question Submitted On: 06/15/2026

Question:

Does the Army prefer white papers that focus on direct Army transition first, commercial market adoption first, or a dual-use path?

Answer:

Please refer to the evaluation criteria listed on the xTech|Inversion Valid Eval signup page for guidance on this.

Question Submitted On: 06/15/2026

Question:

What characteristics distinguish the most successful xTech submissions in previous competitions?

Answer:

Proposals should provide structured, detailed explanations of their proposed solutions while incorporating supporting data, relevant research, and evidence of prior testing or proven performance to establish technical credibility. 

 

Additionally, Clearly and directly address the specified evaluation criteria, enabling reviewers to efficiently verify how the proposed solution meets each dimension. 

Question Submitted On: 06/15/2026

Question:

What level of sponsorship or transition support is provided to winning technologies to bridge the gap after a successful demonstration?

Answer:

The program offers an accelerator for finalists, with additional programming for winners. Furthermore, individuals selected for an SBIR award will be paired with a technical point of contact (who may be the subject matter expert or inventor) for the duration of the contract.

Question Submitted On: 06/15/2026

Question:

Does the Army anticipate opportunities for dual-use commercial technologies that can be adapted for military applications?

Answer:

The xTech Program is always looking for dual-use technologies. For this competition, proposals should focus on developing one of the internal Army IP sets listed in the Request for Information (RFI) and its dual-use potential.

Question Submitted On: 06/15/2026

Question:

Is there a pathway for xTech participation into Army Programs of Record, Other Transaction Authority (OTA) contracts, or operational pilot programs?

Answer:

The transition pathway depends on the specific xTech competition. For this competition, winners will be eligible to submit a Phase I SBIR proposal worth up to $300,000.

Question Submitted On: 06/15/2026

Question:

Are prototype demonstrations expected in laboratory environments, operational environments, or field exercises?

Answer:

Demonstrations are not part of this specific competition. They may, however, be part of follow-on activities for companies that are awarded a Small Business Innovation Research (SBIR) contract. The context for any demonstration would be determined at that time.

Question Submitted On: 06/15/2026

Question:

In inversion, is the attempt to reverse operational assumptions, counter adversary system architectures, or restructure decision and data representation layers?

Answer:

  • Reversing operational assumptions: Yes, this competition is a strategic shift. Instead of the traditional "pull" for custom designs from industry, the Army is "pushing" its existing intellectual property (IP) out to industry for them to develop commercialization plans. 

  • Countering adversary systems: This is considered a secondary benefit. The primary goal is to increase technology transition from Army labs and build relationships with non-traditional partners. 

  • Restructuring data layers: This is also a secondary benefit to the overall goal of shifting from a "pull" to a "push" model for technology transfer.

TECHNICAL POINT OF CONTACT (TPOC)

PROJECTED CMMC LEVEL REQUIREMENT

Level 1

TECHNOLOGY AREAS

Information Systems

MODERNIZATION PRIORITIES

Trusted AI and Autonomy

KEYWORDS

Agentic AI; Digital Engineering; Schema-driven Decision Management; Acquisition Decisions; AI LLM

OBJECTIVE

Prove a decision-as-a-program capability that turns complex engineering/acquisition questions into structured, auditable Decision Packages – faster, with higher confidence.

DESCRIPTION

This topic will prototype and demonstrate a schema-driven Decision Management (DM) foundation plus a governed agentic AI layer that turns messy decision requests into auditable, signer-ready Decision Packages. The focus is proof by demonstration (not a full product build) to show the approach works for point trade studies and long-horizon acquisition decision programs with traceability, robustness, and human control. AI can process vast amounts of structured and unstructured data from Digital Engineering (DE) ecosystems, including digital threads and digital twins, enabling comprehensive analysis across the entire product lifecycle. Interoperability across models is achieved as AI integrates data from various DE tools (e.g., SysML 2.0, UML, etc.) and provides a unified view of system models, enabling cross-functional teams to collaborate effectively.

The first objective is to demonstrate a unified representation that supports both (a) single-episode trade studies and (b) multi-episode "decision programs" with refresh cycles. This includes implementing context engineering specifically for the ground vehicle domain through knowledge graphs and semantic layers that capture domain-specific relationships, constraints, and requirements.

The second objective is to implement agentic capabilities that produce structured artifacts and reproducible outputs, while maintaining human control and predictable behavior per established human-AI interaction guidance. AI will automate the validation of technical documents, models, and outputs, ensuring compliance with standards and requirements throughout the decision-making process.

The third objective is to extend the schema so bias checks, risks, and assumptions are explicit, testable objects – so decision readiness can be assessed before sign-off and refreshed responsibly when conditions change. The system will leverage semantic understanding to maintain consistency across digital engineering artifacts and enable traceable decision rationale.

PHASE I

The Phase 1 Desired Outcomes are as follows:

- A decision schema that makes objectives, options, constraints, assumptions, risks, and bias checks first-class objects

- Agentic AI that: performs structured elicitation into the formal model, then generates decision workflow plans, and executes reproducible evaluation runs with clear “what flips the decision” logic

- Two end-to-end demonstrations showing the approach scales from point-in-time trade studies to long-horizon program decisions with refresh cycles as evidence and assumptions change.

PHASE II

The DoW currently has multiple contractors developing AI/LLM tools for core warfighter purposes. However, little effort has been expended towards an AIgentics decision intelligence capability that supports accelerated commercial acquisition or longer lead traditional development. The DoW is agnostic as to a developed AI commercial package that fulfills adding AIgentics to current AI/LLM for Decision Intelligence for continuous acquisition. During Phase II it is expected that the successful contractor will develop a combined AIgentics and AI/LLM decision intelligence workflow capability with two cases provided from PAE Maneuver Ground and PAE Fires. This software platform needs to be modeled and developed as a commercial open-source platform that both the DoW and commercial enterprises would use for their Product Design & Development (PDD) and acquisition. The current COTS application, DAOSoft, provides an open capability that employs an advanced structured decision/trade study capability with a partially developed AI/LLM decision intelligence workflow. The Army is looking for any and all ideas that can extend or replace current acquisition capabilities and is agnostic to all current solutions. The successful Phase II prototype will be immediately useful, but it is also expected that the contractor would potentially execute follow-on Phase III contracts for individual customer installation. This would be similar to the current best practice deployment of large ERP systems from SAP and Oracle.

PHASE III DUAL USE APPLICATIONS

Potential commercial use cases include the vehicle design process for the automotive industry. The workflow can be relatively similar to the vehicle design process for the Army with some different considerations.

REFERENCES

  1. https://saemobilus.sae.org/papers/concept-execution-ai-agentic-decision-intelligence-framework-product-planning-concept-development-2025-01-0455

Power the space: high-voltage radiation hardened power switches for space power and propulsion

PROJECTED CMMC LEVEL REQUIREMENT

Level 2 (Self)

TECHNOLOGY AREAS

Electronics

MODERNIZATION PRIORITIES

Microelectronics

KEYWORDS

high voltage, high power, radiation hardened (rad hard), power switch, single event burnout, electronics, product design kit (PDK)

OBJECTIVE

The objective of this topic is to build and demonstrate high-voltage radiation hardened semiconductor power switching electronics which enables novel space propulsion technologies (e.g., electrical propulsion) and high-voltage bus lines to advance space high-power systems. The desired results should deliver radiation-hardened (rad-hard) power switches with supplied voltage larger than 350 V up to 1 kV with high efficiency (> 80%).

ITAR

The technology within this topic is restricted under the International Traffic in Arms Regulation (ITAR), 22 CFR Parts 120-130, which controls the export and import of defense-related material and services, including export of sensitive technical data, or the Export Administration Regulation (EAR), 15 CFR Parts 730-774, which controls dual use items. Offerors must disclose any proposed use of foreign nationals (FNs), their country(ies) of origin, the type of visa or work permit possessed, and the statement of work (SOW) tasks intended for accomplishment by the FN(s) in accordance with section 3.5 of the Announcement. Offerors are advised foreign nationals proposed to perform on this topic may be restricted due to the technical data under US Export Control Laws.

DESCRIPTION

Historically, U.S. space dominance relied on a benign environment where assets operated statically to provide communication, intelligence, surveillance, reconnaissance (ISR), and positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT) functions. Today, space is a contested and active warfighting domain. In response, the U.S. Space Force (USSF) is adopting the "Maneuver Without Regret" (MWR) concept. Implementing MWR necessitates high-voltage architectures (200V–800V) to support next-generation Electric Propulsion (EP). Furthermore, space edge computing, a critical microelectronics technology that necessitates increased on-board power, is being developed to enhance autonomous decision-making for threat avoidance. USSF is also advancing Space-Based Solar Power (SBSP), aiming to beam solar energy via microwave or laser to contested terrestrial environments where traditional refueling is restricted. The transition from static to active space postures necessitates the transformation of space power systems. High-voltage (HV) power supplies and bus lines are critical for these applications, as size, weight, and power (SWaP) remain the primary constraints due to launch costs.

To demonstrate HV power systems in space, rad-hard power switches are critical enablers, and the state-of-the-art Si rad-hard power switches are derated to 350 V maximal. Since single event burnouts (SEB) caused by electrical field transience induced by heavy-ion radiation in space is the primary failure mechanism for HV power switches, it is desired to reduce the electrical field within the device through innovations with minimal penalty for the on resistance. Solutions with substantial increase of the on resistance is considered “derating,” which limits the efficiency - an important metric of this topic.

PHASE I

This topic is intended for technology proven ready to move directly into Phase II. Therefore, Phase I awards will not be made for this topic. The applicant is required to provide detail and documentation in the D2P2 proposal which demonstrates accomplishment of a “Phase I-type” effort, including a feasibility study. This includes determining, insofar as possible, the scientific and technical merit and feasibility of ideas appearing to have commercial potential. This feasibility may be demonstrated by providing evidence that the applicant’s device can be fabricated using commercially-viable semiconductor foundry processes, providing a preliminary assessment of space-rated packaging solutions capable of handling both the high voltage and thermal extraction requirements in a vacuum, and/or clear evidence of a combination of advanced TCAD simulations, preliminary bench testing, or other practical demonstrations.

PHASE II

Phase II will focus on the design, fabrication, integration, and demonstration of high-voltage (HV) radiation-hardened (rad-hard) power switching devices capable of enabling next-generation space power switches, preferably through a commercial foundry process that will benefit the commercialization process in Phase III. The rad-hard power switches are expected to pass the 300 krad total ionizing dose standard without failure and need to have SEB immunity at Si linear transfer energy (LET) of 85 MeV cm2/mg with fluence at least 1E6 ions/cm2. It is expected to test SEB immunity in creditable domestic test facilities including but not limited to the NASA Space Radiation Laboratory at Brookhaven National Laboratory. These devices are expect to operate at biased voltage > 600 V during these radiation tests, preferably up to 1 kV. The efficiency of these power switches needs to be at least 80%. Finally, the wafer yield at the end of the Phase II is expected to be above 50%. Proposed solutions need to demonstrate “single event immunity” along with tolerances of other radiation effects (e.g., total ionizing dose) while keeping the power-switch efficiency high.

Phase II efforts should culminate in a prototype and supporting test data package that demonstrates technical performance, radiation survivability, manufacturability, and readiness for transition into Department of the Air Force and U.S. Space Force applications. Deliverables should include sufficient design, fabrication, test, and performance data to support subsequent qualification, packaging, reliability testing, and commercialization activities anticipated during Phase III.

PHASE III DUAL USE APPLICATIONS

Phase III represents the transition and commercialization of the SBIR funded research and development (R&D) efforts into Department of War (DoW) and commercial applications. The expected Phase III efforts involves further maturation and deployment of the developed technology, with the goal of achieving operational readiness and widespread adoption. The desired activities include but are not limited to product design kit (PDK) development, HV package development, and MIL-PRF-19500 screening and Reliability test.

Commercialization opportunities include dual-use applications in commercial satellite systems, in-space transportation, advanced power electronics, and other high-reliability semiconductor markets requiring radiation-hardened high-voltage switching technologies. Successful Phase III efforts should result in a qualified, manufacturable, and commercially sustainable product that enables resilient, maneuverable, and high-power space systems for both government and commercial customers. Successful Phase III efforts are expected to mature the technology from a demonstrated prototype toward a qualified production-ready component suitable for operational integration.

PROJECTED CMMC LEVEL REQUIREMENT

Level 2 (Self)

TECHNOLOGY AREAS

Battlespace  |  Electronics  |  Sensors

MODERNIZATION PRIORITIES

Integrated Sensing and Cyber  |  Trusted AI and Autonomy

KEYWORDS

sensor network, sensors, acoustic, optical, radio frequency, C-sUAS, sneaky drone, RF-silent dark drone, base defense

OBJECTIVE

Innovations in Counter-UAS sensor technologies, data processing, and networking to solve the "sneaky drone" problem by improving the detection, tracking, and identification of small, low-altitude, terrain-masked, and RF-silent Group 1-3 UAS. The system must detect targets from 1 meter up to 300 meters (threshold), 500 meters (objective) off the ground, with individual sensor nodes detecting targets at a horizontal range of at least 100 meters. The nodes must integrate to create at least 10km of combined linear boundary coverage. The final system must cost less than $100k at full-rate production.

DESCRIPTION

This DAF focused open topic seeks C-sUAS detect options for transition into the USAF and USSF, specifically supporting AFLCMC/ES and the JIATF 401 marketplace. This effort seeks low-cost detection and recognition sensors to be configured as a perimeter network for early warning of low-flying drones. The sensors must be able to operate in cluttered environments and recognize non-RF emitting "dark" drones (distinguishing drone vs. not a drone). It must integrate data from all sensors at a node into a single track, providing at least the target's heading along with the absolute location of the detecting node. The system must feature remote node control and be fully controllable via external API commands. The system must be able to integrate into the Medusa C2 or other AF directed C2. Solutions are strictly for permanent base defense applications; therefore, strict SWaP (size and weight) limitations do not apply, and systems can rely on direct or off-grid permanent power.

PHASE I

This is a Direct to Phase 2 (D2P2) topic. Phase I proposals will be rejected. For this D2P2 topic, the Government requires that the applicant will have accomplished the following in a “Phase I-type” effort accomplished outside of the SBIR program through other means. In order to demonstrate this feasibility, the applicant must have developed and validated a working prototype that has been tested in a simulated or non-operational relevant environment. Specifically, the applicant must demonstrate that their system is capable of detecting and tracking non-RF emitting Group 1-3 UAS at low altitudes while outputting basic track and sensor node location data.

PHASE II

Transition to AFLCMC/ES and the JIATF-401 C-UAS marketplace for Base Defense. Commercial dual-use applications include airport security, critical infrastructure protection, and border patrol.

PHASE III DUAL USE APPLICATIONS

Transition to AFLCMC/ES and the JIATF-401 C-UAS marketplace for Base Defense. Commercial dual-use applications include airport security, critical infrastructure protection, and border patrol

PROJECTED CMMC LEVEL REQUIREMENT

Level 2 (Self)

TECHNOLOGY AREAS

Space Platforms

MODERNIZATION PRIORITIES

Space Technology

KEYWORDS

SpaceWERX, On-Orbit Cyber Defense; Space Vehicles (SVs); Autonomous Cyber Response; Real-Time Monitoring; Defensive Cyber Warfare (DCW); Artificial Intelligence (AI); Machine Learning (ML); Threat Simulation

OBJECTIVE

SpaceWERX, in partnership with Cyberspace Warfare professionals within the U.S. Space Force (USSF), are seeking innovative solutions supporting the next generation capabilities to defend space systems from adversarial attack through the cyber domain. The desired outcome is to produce capabilities that advance the domain of defensive cyber warfare operations in 8 different focus areas. Each focus area presents a unique opportunity for industry to develop innovative solutions and provide critical capabilities to the USSF. This initiative supports the USSF’s broader strategy to generate, present, sustain, and improve Cyberspace Warfare forces for the Joint Force.

ITAR

The technology within this topic is restricted under the International Traffic in Arms Regulation (ITAR), 22 CFR Parts 120-130, which controls the export and import of defense-related material and services, including export of sensitive technical data, or the Export Administration Regulation (EAR), 15 CFR Parts 730-774, which controls dual use items. Offerors must disclose any proposed use of foreign nationals (FNs), their country(ies) of origin, the type of visa or work permit possessed, and the statement of work (SOW) tasks intended for accomplishment by the FN(s) in accordance with section 3.5 of the Announcement. Offerors are advised foreign nationals proposed to perform on this topic may be restricted due to the technical data under US Export Control Laws.

DESCRIPTION

The USSF’s defensive cyber operations mission is focused on the rapid integration of capabilities into the Defensive Cyber Warfare (DCW) pipeline to address unique and complex cybersecurity requirements for space systems. This effort aims to enable the scaling of current DCW systems for widespread protection and to improve USSF operational readiness. Modernizing Defensive Cyber Warfare for Space requires shifting from fragmented, reactive security to a cohesive, intelligence-driven posture that spans from the commercial supply chain to the orbital edge. This initiative is seeking to build a unified defense ecosystem where AI-enhanced vetting ensures the integrity of hardware and software long before deployment. Once operational, agile data architectures will seamlessly normalize complex telemetry across hybrid networks, fueling advanced machine learning engines to autonomously detect and intercept threats in real time. The focus areas should optimize the existing IT environment to minimize cost and maximize efficiency. By extending these lightweight, resilient safeguards directly onto spacecraft and disconnected ground infrastructure, and validating them through hyper-realistic, immersive training environments, this initiative aims to equip cyber operators with a decisive, end-to-end advantage against advanced adversaries. The initiative is organized around eight primary focus areas to address critical technical challenges:

  1. Focus Area #1: Lightweight and Cloud-Agnostic Data Ingest
    1. Develop a cohesive, high-throughput data ingestion solution for on-premises and cloud environments that is infrastructure-agnostic.
  2. Focus Area #2: Defensive Cyber Warfare Systems - Proactive Software Assurance and Malware Detection
    1.  Deliver automated security vetting for third-party software, generating Software Bill of Materials (SBOMs) and conducting risk assessments to identify vulnerabilities.
  3. Focus Area #3: On-Orbit Space Vehicle Cyber Defense and Monitoring
    1. Seek software-based capabilities with minimal Size, Weight, and Power (WaP) for advanced on-satellite monitoring and autonomous response directly on Space Vehicles.
  4. Focus Area #4: Immersive Space Cyber Test Environment
    1. Establish high-fidelity test platforms, integrating simulated assets like digital twins and ground systems for operator training.
  5. Focus Area #5: Adaptive Data Parsers and Transformation Engine
    1. Build adaptive engines capable of universally ingesting and normalizing diverse data types into standardized formats for DCW analytics.
  6. Focus Area #6: AI-Driven Cyber Threat Detection
    1. Leverage Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) for behavior-based threat detection to identify anomalies across multi-domain data sources in bandwidth-constrained environments.
  7. Focus Area #7: AI-Driven Digital Supply Chain Illumination and Risk Management
    1. Deliver analytical tools providing deep, multi-tier visibility to identify threats ranging from cyber risks to geopolitical vulnerabilities.
  8. Focus Area #8: Portable Edge Cyber Defense Kit
    1. Deliver self-contained, plug-and-play kits for threat detection and response in disconnected, intermittent, and low-bandwidth (DIL) environments.

PHASE I

This topic is intended for technology proven ready to move directly into Phase II. Therefore, Phase I awards will not be made for this topic. The applicant is required to provide detail and documentation in the Direct-to-Phase-II (D2P2) proposal which demonstrates accomplishment of a “Phase I-type” effort, including a feasibility study. This includes determining, insofar as possible, the scientific and technical merit and feasibility of ideas appearing to have commercial potential. It must have validated the product-mission fit between the proposed solution and a potential U.S. Air Force (USAF) and/or USSF stakeholder. The applicant should have defined a clear, immediately actionable plan with the proposed solution and the U.S. Department of the Air Force (DAF) customer and end-user. The feasibility study should have:

  1. Clearly identified the potential stakeholders of the adapted solution for solving the USAF and/or USSF need(s).
  2. Described the pathway to integrating with DAF operations, to include how the applicant plans to accomplish core technology development, navigate applicable regulatory processes, and integrate with other relevant systems and/or processes.
  3. Describe if and how the solution can be used by other U.S. Department of Defense (DoD) or Governmental customers.

PHASE II

Proposed solutions should develop and demonstrate innovative technologies to support operations as part of the USSF’s cyberspace warfare for space operations. Solutions should address one or more of the following 8 focus areas:

Focus Area #1: Lightweight and Cloud-Agnostic Data Ingest

To support future-ready data operations for Defensive Cyber Warfare (DCW) systems, the team is seeking innovative solutions that enable best value, lightweight and efficient data ingestion at the edge or at the hub. A primary challenge is significant infrastructure overhead associated with traditional data capture methods. Solutions are sought that can be deployed with minimal impact to existing systems, providing high-throughput data capture without demanding extensive hardware or complex configurations. The goal is to establish a solution for pulling critical data into analytics platforms, ensuring that on-prem monitoring capabilities are both effective and sustainable.

In parallel, this effort is also interested in addressing data ingestion for cloud environments. Proposed solutions should explore potential Cloud Service Provider (CSP) agnostic approaches that offer flexible and scalable data ingestion independent of cloud provider solutions. This includes exploring technologies such as virtual TAPs (vTAPs). The ultimate objective is a cohesive data ingest solution that is independent of the underlying infrastructure, whether it be on-prem, in a single cloud, or across a multi-cloud landscape.

Focus Area #2: Defensive Cyber Warfare Systems - Proactive Software Assurance and Malware Detection

To safeguard Defensive Cyber Warfare (DCW) systems against an increasingly compromised global software supply chain, the team is seeking advanced capabilities for the deep inspection and security vetting of third-party software packages. This initiative is twofold, addressing the unique challenges posed by both Free and Open-Source Software (FOSS) and non-approved Commercial Off-the-Shelf (COTS) products. The goal is to proactively identify and mitigate threats before they are introduced into critical operational environments.

Solutions should be capable of thoroughly evaluating FOSS packages to provide a comprehensive Software Bill of Materials (SBOM) and detailed risk analysis. This capability should automatically alert operators to a range of security concerns, including embedded malware, hidden back-doors, and vulnerabilities corresponding to the Open Worldwide Application Security Project (OWASP) Top 10. A key feature will be the ability to trace the software's origin and development lineage, providing critical intelligence on contributions from foreign entities or known adversaries. A similar vetting mechanism is desired for COTS software not currently on an Approved Product List (APL). This system should leverage innovative techniques such as binary analysis, SBOM generation, or other advanced methods to produce a thorough risk assessment, alerting on both specific security vulnerabilities and broader digital supply chain risks. These detection mechanisms would provide the greatest value if implemented for validation onboard or integrated prior to space system deployment.

Focus Area #3: On-Orbit Space Vehicle Cyber Defense and Monitoring

The team is seeking the development of an advanced, on-orbit detection and response capability for Space Vehicles (SVs) to directly reduce or negate the impact of cyber-attacks on critical space systems. The primary objective is to deploy a persistent monitoring solution directly onto the SV that can identify and, in approved instances, autonomously respond to malicious activity in real-time. This onboard capability should be designed for seamless integration with existing ground-based Defensive Cyber Warfare (DCW) systems, ensuring that all telemetry and alert data are relayed to terrestrial monitoring centers.

Proposed solutions should be capable of monitoring a wide spectrum of the SV’s internal functions. This includes, but is not limited to: detecting unauthorized software, firmware, or critical configuration changes; monitoring traffic on essential, non-redundant components such as the 1553 Bus and SpaceWire; and identifying anomalous behavior such as irregular commands or malware uploads. Furthermore, the system should be sensitive to threat indicators targeting the vehicle’s core subsystems, including triggers related to power manipulation, system timing interference, or unauthorized payload function commands. Upon detecting an approved event, the system should be capable of executing a direct response on the SV and transmitting comprehensive logs to the ground segment for analysis.

Given the highly restrictive nature of space platforms, solutions should be engineered with minimal size, weight, and power (SWaP) impact. Software-based solutions that impose a negligible resource footprint on the host vehicle are strongly preferred. Offerors should be aware that development and testing will likely be conducted using high-fidelity environments such as a FlatSat or realistic simulations.

Focus Area #4: Immersive Space Cyber Test Environment

The team is seeking the development of a comprehensive and immersive test and purple teaming platform designed to prepare cyber operators for the unique challenges of defending space systems against advanced cyber threats. The objective is to create a realistic, hands-on environment where operators can develop and hone their skills in detecting and responding to attacks targeting space assets and their supporting infrastructure. This capability will be instrumental in building a proficient and mission-ready cyber defense workforce.

The proposed solution should include the creation of two core high-fidelity components: a simulated space asset, which could be a physical FlatSat or a sophisticated digital twin, and a corresponding simulated ground system. The ground simulation should realistically model all essential elements, including the ground control segment, remote tracking stations, and antenna systems. A critical requirement is the full integration of the government-furnished Defensive Cyber Warfare (DCW) tool suite, allowing operators to train with the actual systems they will use in live missions.

Furthermore, the training platform should come equipped with a robust curriculum of realistic, scenario-based cyber-attacks. These scenarios will serve as the foundation for training exercises and should simulate a range of credible threats, including but not limited to: direct cyber-attacks against the space vehicle's onboard systems, attacks targeting the ground control systems, and threats aimed at compromising the communication and access links between the space and ground segments.

Focus Area #5: Adaptive Data Parsers and Transformation Engine

The team is seeking solutions for a universal parser or data transformation mechanism capable of ingesting and normalizing a wide array of data types into a single, standardized format for seamless integration into the Defensive Cyber Warfare (DCW) analytics systems.

Developing dedicated parsers for each data source is time consuming, labor intensive, and leads to significant code maintenance challenges. To address this, there is a need for an adaptive data parsing or transformation engine that can handle a wide range of data types used in analytics: including space specific protocols, proprietary logs from various network devices, proprietary data types produced by cyber tools, and non-standard formats from numerous intelligence threat feeds. The solution should minimize code maintenance when new Security Information and Event Management (SIEMs) or data structures are introduced and should support the incorporation of new data formats without requiring major code revisions. By transforming disparate data into a common, query-able format, the solution will significantly enhance analytical capabilities and provide a comprehensive, correlated view of the battlespace. This capability is essential for creating a unified and consistent data pipeline, which is fundamental for effective security monitoring, threat hunting, and incident response.

Focus Area #6: AI-Driven Cyber Threat Detection

In response to the emerging adversarial tactics, the team recognizes that traditional signature-based detection methods are no longer sufficient to provide a decisive advantage and are seeking to augment Defensive Cyber Warfare (DCW) systems with an advanced, behavior-based threat detection capability. This solution should leverage artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), or advanced heuristics to establish a baseline of normal activity and proactively identify anomalies indicative of a compromise.

To address this need, enhanced AI/ML driven threat detection and analysis is required, including anomaly detection across multi domain data sources such as network, host, user, and space specific telemetry; automated threat hunting that correlates disparate indicators to reveal hidden patterns; predictive analytics that identify potential attack vectors before they are exploited; and natural language processing that can automatically analyze and correlate intelligence from multiple threat feeds. Additionally, AI/ML capabilities should be trained in an operational-like environment to reduce noise and optimize detection capabilities. The AI/ML capabilities should also be able to operate effectively in bandwidth constrained or contested environments common in space operations. Automated triage and prioritization of alerts is needed to reduce analyst fatigue and speed response times, along with AI assisted incident response recommendations informed by historical attack patterns and mission context.

Focus Area #7: AI-Driven Digital Supply Chain Illumination and Risk Management

The team is seeking a comprehensive digital supply chain risk management capability to safeguard the flow of software and hardware from vendors and suppliers. In an era of interconnected, global supply networks, proposed solutions are needed that leverage Artificial Intelligence (AI) and advanced analytical tools to provide deep, multi-tier visibility and proactive risk identification across the entire supplier ecosystem.

This capability should continuously monitor and analyze a wide range of data sources to deliver real-time intelligence on potential disruptions. This includes detecting cybersecurity risks, such as data breaches or attacks within a supplier's network, as well as broader supplier and operational risks, including material shortages, production delays, financial instability, or legal and labor issues. The system should use AI to identify and alert on emerging threats that could impact the ecosystem, allowing us to protect against both immediate cyber threats and long-term operational disruptions. By creating a unified view of the supply chain and automating the detection of vulnerabilities, this capability will enable us to move from a reactive to a predictive and resilient posture, ensuring the integrity and continuity of DCW systems.

Focus Area #8: Portable Edge Cyber Defense Kit

The team is seeking a lightweight, portable, and plug-and-play "fly-away" kit for cyber threat detection, investigation, and response at remote and forward-deployed locations. As operations increasingly extend into austere environments, the USSF seeks solutions for a self-contained capability that can function effectively with limited or nonexistent network connectivity. The solution should address the challenge of providing robust cyber defense in disconnected, intermittent, and low-bandwidth (DIL) settings where reliance on centralized security infrastructure is not feasible. This Edge Cyber Kit will empower operators to conduct local threat hunting and initial remediation, ensuring the security of critical assets at the tactical edge.

The proposed solution should be engineered with a minimal physical footprint (size, weight, and power) to ensure portability and ease of deployment. It should possess the onboard processing and analytical power to autonomously detect and investigate threats without real-time reach-back. A critical requirement is sufficient internal storage to collect and securely hold logs, forensic data, and other mission-critical artifacts for extended periods. This stored data must be easily transferable, allowing operators to push it to central analysis platforms for deeper, post-mission analysis upon their return to a connected environment. The kit should provide an intuitive interface that enables an operator to effectively manage incidents and secure networks in the field, bridging the gap between disconnected operations and enterprise-level situational awareness.

PHASE III DUAL USE APPLICATIONS

Potential Phase III efforts will pursue transition of the capability to operational use through non-SBIR/STTR funding streams, aiming for a Technology Readiness Level (TRL) of 6 or 7 and demonstrating functionality in relevant environments. Phase II efforts that demonstrate technical maturity, integration feasibility, and mission alignment may be selected for continued development and deployment into operational environments.

During Phase III, performers may be expected to:

- Advance System Readiness

- Demonstrate Operational Capability

- Enable Cross-Service Application

- Pursue Dual-Use Commercialization

Phase III work may be performed with non-SBIR/STTR funding and can include further government-sponsored prototyping, operational transition activities, or commercialization via strategic partners in the defense and aerospace sectors.

REFERENCES

  1. TRL Guide - https://www.gao.gov/assets/gao-20-48g.pdf.

Question Submitted On: 09/04/2026

Question:

Questions regarding DAF26BX06-DV512, Focus Area #5: Adaptive Data Parsers and Transformation Engine

 

  1. Has the Government selected or preferred a canonical data model, ontology, or standardized output schema for normalized Defensive Cyber Warfare data, or should offerors propose and justify their own common data model? If a preferred model exists, will its required fields, metadata, and interface specifications be furnished to awardees?
  2. Will the Government provide representative unclassified, sanitized, or synthetic datasets, interface-control documents, schemas, or a DCW integration test harness during Phase II? If operational samples cannot be provided, may offerors use traceable synthetic data mapped to published standards to demonstrate technical feasibility?
  3. How will the Government evaluate whether a parser or transformation engine is “adaptive” or “universal”? Would onboarding a new format through declarative configuration, schema mapping, or an isolated plug-in—without modifying the core engine—satisfy the intent, or is automated format inference expected?
  4. Are there desired quantitative performance thresholds for Focus Area #5, including sustained and burst event throughput, concurrent data-source count, maximum payload size, transformation latency, acceptable rejection rates, and zero-loss or backpressure requirements?
  5. What evidence will the Government consider sufficient to demonstrate completion of a Phase I-type feasibility effort for this focus area? Specifically, is there a preferred minimum number or diversity of source formats, benchmark duration, normalization-accuracy measure, end-user validation activity, or integration demonstration?


 

Answer:

  1. The Government has not prescribed a single vendor-specific canonical data model or ontology for this topic. Offerors should propose and justify an extensible, interoperable common data model that preserves original source data, context, and metadata and supports normalization, correlation, search, analytics, and detection. The proposed approach should support reliable mapping to commonly used cybersecurity data models and the Government’s selected data and analytics platform without unnecessary vendor lock-in. Applicable field mappings, interface specifications, and Government-controlled integration requirements will be provided to selected performer(s), as appropriate.
  2. Relevant Government datasets and available integration artifacts may be furnished to selected performer(s) during Phase II, subject to availability and applicable security, access, handling, and distribution requirements. The Government does not guarantee that operational samples or a Government-provided integration test harness will be available. Where representative Government data cannot be provided, offerors may use traceable synthetic or sanitized data mapped to relevant published standards and representative DCW use cases to demonstrate technical feasibility. Specific data, interfaces, schemas, test criteria, and integration mechanisms will be coordinated with selected performer(s), as applicable.
  3. The Government will assess “adaptive” or “universal” based on the solution’s demonstrated ability to onboard diverse, previously unsupported, or changing data formats while minimizing specialized manual analysis, custom development, and modifications to the core engine. Relevant considerations include onboarding time, required human effort, parsing accuracy, resilience to format changes, validation capabilities, and extensibility across protocol and data types. Declarative configuration, schema mapping, or isolated plug-ins may satisfy the intent when the approach materially accelerates onboarding and avoids modification of the core engine. Fully autonomous format inference is not necessarily required; however, offerors should describe and demonstrate how automation, including AI/ML where appropriate, assists with format characterization, parser or transformation generation, validation, and adaptation to previously unseen or evolving data.
  4. The Government has not established uniform quantitative thresholds for all Focus Area #5 use cases. Current operational environments may receive aggregated network traffic at rates up to approximately 40 Gbps; however, the throughput presented to a parser or transformation engine will depend on its architectural placement, source types, and whether it processes raw traffic, extracted data, or derived events. Offerors should provide measured sustained and burst performance, supported source concurrency and payload limits, transformation latency, rejection and error-handling behavior, backpressure and buffering mechanisms, data-loss characteristics, and associated compute requirements. Proposed solutions should demonstrate horizontal scalability and the ability to accommodate growth beyond the initial operational baseline. Specific performance objectives and representative test conditions will be coordinated with selected performer(s) during Phase II.
  5. The maximum character limit for this response has been reached. Question #5 will be resubmitted and answered on the platform separately.

Answer:

The intended end users are U.S. Space Force Cyber Force Elements (CFEs), trained and equipped through their supporting Cyberspace Operations Squadron (CYS). CFEs conduct defensive cyberspace operations in support of Space Force mission systems and may be employed across a range of ground-system environments.
